Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Da Fu, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
At that time, Mañjuśrī manifested as the Great Vidyārāja named Yamāntaka,
his entire body blazing with intense light,
most fierce and utterly terrifying, causing all the other Vidyārājas—
Terrified by the falling of weapons, gods, humans,
and asuras join their palms in fear; all together they take refuge, pay homage,
and offer praise by the tens of millions, beholding this great mass of blazing light.
With a mind tormented by heat like fire, he spoke these words:
"I pray only that the Great Radiant King will cause this great evil omen to cease;
may his light, blazing with great intensity, shine throughout the ten directions."
The devas and humans of the three realms, As well as the asuras and others, Were struck with awe and took refuge in the Triple Gem; They prostrated to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
At that moment, the Great Vidyārāja Assumed a form that quelled evil and transformed it into goodness.
Endowed with great majesty and power, the emanations of Mañjuśrī,
including devas, asuras, and others, all addressed the Great Vidyārāja,
saying: "How should one practice diligence and perform various services?"
Through respectful offerings and the like, one attains great joy;
for this purpose, he has expounded these skillful means to sever our doubts.
At that time, the Great Wrathful One, King Yamāntaka—
Having heard these words, he addressed the devas, asuras, and others:
"Each of you possesses great majesty and virtue; take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, whose merit is supreme, and faithfully obey the Tathāgata’s command."
To benefit all sentient beings, I shall cease my great malevolent form and transform it into a wondrous and auspicious appearance.
Those who have already taken the three refuges should resolve upon bodhicitta; this is my fundamental teaching.
The Great Illumination Sādhana: The phrases for accomplishment such as these— of seven syllables, ten syllables, and so forth—
All devas, humans, and asuras alike, You all should uphold and maintain them.
All aspirations shall be fully accomplished.
This is the root teaching of the wrathful Yamāntaka, which I have personally proclaimed;
at that time, the great earth shook and the oceans and rivers all boiled over.
All devas and humans, yakṣas and rākṣasas, as well as piśācas—
trembling both in body and mind with fear of the Great Vidyārāja—
they each give rise to a heart of reverence.
With palms joined, they all prostrate; they uphold the Great Wrathful King Yamāntaka,
taking his root heart-mantra as the protector of the True Dharma within those three realms.
Within the realm of all humans and devas, this ritual procedure for accomplishment is the most supreme and foremost;
King Yamāntaka himself proclaimed it for all devas and humans.
With faith and acceptance, all rejoice; in the heavens and among humans, they pay homage with their heads bowed in reverence.
Hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas, practicing according to the Dharma, extensively carry out acts of loving-kindness and compassion.
Thus concludes the first section on accomplishment from the *Mañjuśrī-mūla-viśuddhi-vidhi*, this great teaching.
Section Two: The Ritual for Accomplishment in the Maṇḍala of Yamāntaka-Bhairava. Furthermore, the ritual for the supreme maṇḍala.
It can instill great terror within the triple world and can bestow the fulfillment of all requested wishes.
This is called the *Bhīṣmadattaka-maṇḍala-sādhana*.
The practitioner of vidyā first must select a place according to their preference—
whether beneath a great tree, within a śītavana (charnel ground),
inside an empty house, or beside a crossroads.
Either in a mountain valley, or between two stūpas,
or within a grove, or on a mountain peak,
or on a riverbank or seashore, or within a cow-pen.
Whether on a battlefield, at a temple of Maheśvara, or in any secluded place according to one's own inclination,
one should construct the maṇḍala;
furthermore, it must be purified according to the ritual rules.
Within that site, all impure objects such as thorns, tiles, stones, gravel, bones, hair, stakes, wood,
and the like must be completely removed. Thereafter,
one should smear the ground of the maṇḍala with *gomaya* mixed with water purified by the five medicinal herbs.
Then the vidyādhara, having stayed overnight, bathed,
and maintained the purity of the fast and precepts with single-minded devotion,
recited this great vidyā-mantra to effect self-protection.
Furthermore, using either *tūla* cotton or hemp,
one should join three strands of thread to mark out the four directions of the maṇḍala,
beginning first from the east.
Having thus laid out the lines according to the ritual sequence for the four cardinal directions and four intermediate corners,
one should use funeral ashes to fashion four gates at the four cardinal directions and four intermediate corners of the maṇḍala.
Only the southern gate is opened, while the other three remain closed.
In the center of the maṇḍala, draw a lotus flower with colored powder.
Then, beginning from the northeast corner, proceed according to the sequence of the ritual rules.
Using funeral ashes, one should draw the various sages and holy ones, as well as the insignia of the precious staff.
At each of the four gates of the maṇḍala,
one should draw the form of a bhairava.
In the center, upon a lotus, paint the fifth Bhairava form, adorned with skulls; such is the mandala.
Each [item] must be provided in full according to the ritual manual.
Furthermore, there are eight kinds of maṇḍalas;
among them is the maṇḍala one cubit (hasta) in width.
A maṇḍala two cubits wide is for the rite of constant offering;
a maṇḍala three cubits wide is for the rites of averting calamity and increasing prosperity;
and a maṇḍala [of the same width] is for the rite of dispatching the *śatru*.
A maṇḍala four cubits wide is for the rite of attraction and summoning;
a maṇḍala five cubits wide is for the rite of averting calamities and curing illness;
a maṇḍala six cubits wide is for the rite of removing māras and planetary influences.
A maṇḍala seven cubits wide is for the rite of summoning and captivating all the devas;
a maṇḍala eight cubits wide is for the rite of accomplishing all that is sought.
If one constructs [the mandala] at more than eight cubits in this manner,
it will certainly not be accomplished unless it is based on the ritual procedures.
Once the Vidyādhara has drawn the maṇḍala, [he should proceed as follows].
Fill one bowl with scented water;
fill another bowl with various kinds of exquisite flowers,
as well as agallochum, sandalwood, frankincense, ghee lamps, and oil lamps.
If one arranges [the ritual] according to the sequence of the dharma in this manner,
one will certainly attain accomplishment.
Furthermore, one may also perform the rite of the Great Malevolent Maṇḍala.
The Vidyādhara should use *nirvāsa* as the lamp;
he should produce wine, meat, fish, and various kinds of food and drink for the ritual.
Then, the practitioner should prostrate to all the Buddhas and generate the bodhicitta.
At that time, the vidyādhara, according to the ritual,
should himself paint the forms and emblems of the noble deities within the maṇḍala; however,
if he is unable to paint them, [he may employ an artist].
Visualize according to the ritual method:
upon the lotus of the maṇḍala is a subtle syllable,
which transforms into Bhṛkuṭī.
Furthermore, visualize a jeweled staff at each of the four corners of the maṇḍala and a *bhairava* at each of the four gates;
then recite the great vidyā-mantra of *Bhairava*.
Having recited thus,
one should further visualize the eight insignia within the maṇḍala,
which are named: haṃsita, pannaśira, saṃkha, dundubhi, kharpara, cakra, śaṅkhamukhī, and narmadā.
Having visualized in this manner,
one recites this great vidyā-mantra to bring [the deity] into manifestation.
Thereafter, one invokes the Great Wrathful Vidyārāja Yamāntaka.
He enters into his own heart;
his body is black in color with a most terrifying appearance,
endowed with great majesty, and his entire body is ablaze with flames.
Each of the six faces has three eyes;
the eyes are reddish-yellow in color,
and both the hair and the eyebrows are likewise reddish-yellow.
Six feet; his feet trample upon the bhairavas; twelve arms.
The first right hand performs the *varada-mudrā* (gesture of granting boons);
the second holds a hook; the third holds a trident;
and the fourth holds a sword.
The fifth hand holds a precious staff;
the sixth hand holds a battle-axe;
the first left hand holds a skull-cup.
The second hand holds a banner;
the third hand holds a *dumaraṅga* lute; the fourth hand holds a noose;
and the fifth hand has its index finger raised.
The sixth hand holds a jeweled staff;
he wears a garland made of human heads, half-dry and half-moist,
and is adorned with a tiger-skin garment.
His body is massive and his belly broad;
his face displays various wrathful expressions,
with a fierce complexion shifting like a surging ocean.
The manifested forms are indeterminate:
they may appear as wrathful forms, or as benevolent forms;
they may appear as forms of great malice, or as forms of terror.
Alternatively, one may open the mouth and extend the tongue, or expose the teeth;
likewise, when painting with colored powders according to the ritual, the visualization is performed in the same manner.
Having visualized in this way:
Offer scented water as arghya and red flowers upon the crown of the bhūta;
furthermore, use red sandalwood, flowers, and flower garlands.
Offer it at the crown of the head of the Vidyārāja Yamāntaka,
while reciting the Great Heart-Mantra of the Vidyārāja Yamāntaka;
the vidyādhara should then perform the visualization.
This heart-mantra of the vidyārāja enters one’s own heart;
reciting the head-mantra, one visualizes it upon the head;
reciting the crown-mantra, one visualizes it upon the crown.
Recite the mantra of the armor and visualize it as armor.
Having performed this visualization,
recite the mantra of incense and offer the incense.
Thereafter, one should offer lamps lit at each of the four cardinal directions and four intermediate corners of the maṇḍala,
using various kinds of food and drink, as well as the most excellent incense and flowers.
Offer to the wrathful vidyārāja Yamanataka;
furthermore, generate various kinds of food and drink and offer them to the bhūtas and all other spirits.
Furthermore, take a bowl filled with pure water and a bowl filled with excellent incense and place them outside the maṇḍala. Then,
according to the ritual, cause the disciple receiving the dharma to bathe and become thoroughly purified.
He then recited the Great Mantra of the Wrathful Vidyārāja to consecrate a single flower,
and had the disciple hold this flower with the fingers of both hands while covering his head and face with a cloth.
While reciting the names of the Three Jewels,
the ācārya leads the disciple into the maṇḍala and causes him to make a vow;
he then casts a flower into the center of the maṇḍala.
Having removed the face-cloth, the master and the disciple recognize the *iṣṭadevatā*.
The *ācārya* then explains to the disciple the mudrās of the precious staff and the secret samaya-mudrās of the Three Jewels.
Immediately, one pours fragrant flowers and water over the disciple’s crown.
One further makes offerings of fragrant flowers and bestows upon the disciple the heart-mantra of the wrathful vidyārāja.
At that time, once the disciple has received the Great Illumination (mahāvidyā),
he shall prostrate with his head at the feet [of the master] and offer gifts and worship to the ācārya according to his ability.
Whatever the disciple desires shall certainly be accomplished.
Furthermore, place a bowl filled with scented water at the eastern side of the maṇḍala and offer arghya water to the Vidyārāja.
At that time, the ācārya shall recite the great mantra for dispatching.
Dispatch the Great Wrathful Vidyārāja Yamāntaka back to his original station.
Offer arghya water to the maṇḍala.
In this manner, perform these rites constantly according to the dharma.
One shall be able to attain vast and peerless merit in the world.

extensively pacifying calamities, eliminating afflictions, and increasing the merit, fortune, and lifespan of sentient beings.
This person will before long attain unsurpassed enlightenment and will certainly achieve accomplishment in the great vidyā-ritual of the Vidyārāja Yamāntaka.
When the vidyādhara performs this rite, [the result follows].
Having paid respectful homage before the sacred image and so forth, sit in a composed manner.
Then recite the Great Mantra while pronouncing your own name:
"I, [Name], for the sake of another, [Name], and others..."
By performing the rites for pacifying calamities and increasing prosperity, one attains the accomplishments sought.
Thus, by further reciting the great mantra one thousand times,
one immediately achieves the pacification of misfortunes and the increase of virtuous merit.
If one seeks to pacify calamities for kings, cities, provincial capitals, or settlements,
one should recite the Great Mantra two thousand times.
If one seeks to pacify calamities for elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and so forth, [one should likewise recite it].
Recite the Great Mantra one thousand times.
If one seeks to pacify calamities for the sake of all sentient beings,
reciting the Great Mantra one ayuta times will bring accomplishment in every case.
Furthermore, regarding the method for increasing and accomplishing:
the vidyādhara, according to the ritual,
should place a clean vessel filled with excellent milk before the Vidyārāja.
Using exquisite flowers smeared with white sandalwood incense,
empower them one thousand times and cast them into the vessel of milk.
The Vidyādhara recites the name: "I,
so-and-so, for the sake of such-and-so another,
seek the accomplishment of all desired aims for the purpose of increase."
Furthermore, regarding the method for achieving the accomplishment of wealth and nobility:
the vidyādhara should first practice altruistic deeds with a mind of loving-kindness and perform a great offering according to the previously described ritual procedure.
Burn aloeswood incense and offer fine flowers soaked in white sandalwood incense daily;
by thus making offerings and reciting the mantra, one will immediately attain great wealth.
Alternatively, a vidyādhara may follow the aforementioned ritual procedure.
Having recited "Namo svāhā" one hundred times,
one should go to the seashore or enter the Gaṅgā River with the water reaching the navel.
Using white lotus flowers smeared with white sandalwood incense,
recite the Great Mantra to empower them;
by casting them into a river one hundred thousand times (one *lakṣa*), one will attain great wealth and nobility.
Alternatively, by using red lotuses smeared with red sandalwood and performing the ritual as previously described,
one may cast them into a river and obtain an inexhaustible treasure trove.
Or, the vidyādhara may use *adhimuktaka* flowers.
Performing the ritual as previously described, throw [the items] into the river;
upon completing one *lakṣa* [of repetitions], one will obtain one *lakṣa* of gold coins.
Alternatively, according to the aforementioned method, throw flowers three *lakṣas* of times.
It can also subdue all yakṣiṇīs and accomplish all feats according to the practitioner’s intent. Alternatively,
the vidyādhara may proceed as before according to the ritual rules.
Using high-quality *jāti* flowers smeared with white sandalwood incense,
one should cast them into a river for one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*).
Then, whatever one seeks within the great earth shall be obtained.
Furthermore, regarding the accomplishment:
having smeared white lotus flowers with the three kinds of honey and performed the homa according to the ritual rules, [the rite is accomplished].
That blessed deity will appear in their own form and grant all wishes.
Furthermore, here is the method for accomplishment.
Performing homa by burning ghee and honey for seven days and nights,
one obtains seven great villages.
Furthermore, the method for accomplishment:
Perform one hundred thousand *homa* offerings using the five grains and clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
One will obtain inexhaustible wealth and jewels and be able to accomplish all tasks.
Furthermore, there is another method for accomplishment.
Perform one hundred thousand *homa* offerings using auspicious fruits;
one will obtain great profit and sustenance among both gods and humans.
Furthermore, the method for accomplishment is as follows:
Using fresh *nūlība* grass mixed with cow’s milk,
one should recite the Great Mantra and the syllable *svāhā*.
One will thereby obtain an extended lifespan.
Furthermore, as for the method of accomplishment:
kindle a fire using *bhallātaka* wood and perform *homa* with clarified butter.
If one performs this rite daily in this manner, it will increase one's lifespan and augment one's wisdom.

One will possess great power, remember clearly without forgetting, and be praised by all. If one performs *homa* using all kinds of food and drink, one will likewise attain great power, and one's fame will spread so that all people praise them; everything one desires will be accomplished.

Regarding the seven to ten syllables of the Great Illuminator (Mahāvidyā) that have been taught:
they cause the vidyādhara to practice recitation according to the ritual rules in a secluded place, performing the conduct of fearlessness.
All desired aims shall be accomplished.
Now, the great mantra of the single syllable HŪṂ is taught.
The vidyādhara, practicing according to the ritual, should recite it while performing the fearless conduct.
The dharma sought shall certainly be accomplished.
This present syllable HŪṂ is the subtle heart-mantra of the Vidyārāja Yamāntaka;
it possesses great majestic power and inconceivable merit.
It can bring auspiciousness to the practitioner; if one first maintains ten lakṣas,
reciting each of the seven syllables according to the preceding ritual rules,
all that is sought shall be accomplished.
Furthermore, regarding the syllable Oṃ:
by reciting it according to the ritual rules before a painted image of the Vidyārāja,
one will certainly attain accomplishment.
Furthermore, regarding the painted image:
one should use a piece of silk approximately one cubit in length;
having washed it clean with water, [proceed as follows].
Anoint it with excellent incense and use superior pigments to paint the Vidyārāja Yamāntaka,
his body the color of blue clouds and his face bearing the appearance of great, fierce wrath.
His face has three eyes and is reddish-yellow in color.
His hair stands upright and is also reddish-yellow.
He is adorned with a skull and wears a tiger-skin garment.
His entire body is completely filled with blazing flames.
He rides upon a water buffalo and has two hands and two feet.
His right hand holds a staff, and his left hand forms the *kṛtāñjali* (threatening) mudrā.
Having first painted various offerings,
and having thus completed the painting,
the vidyādhara should first offer incense, flowers, food, and drink with a single-minded devotion.
Thereafter, enter a stone cave and unfurl the painted image.
Prostrate yourself in worship and sit upright and composed before the image, reciting with a focused and sincere mind.
When the painted image on the cloth begins to move, smiles, or emits light—
upon the appearance of such auspicious signs, one attains true accomplishment (*siddhi*).
At that time, the vidyādhara becomes possessed of great auspiciousness and is able to perform all activities.
They can shatter mountains and exhaust the rivers and great oceans;
they can dispatch demons and summon dragons and devas.
All such deeds as these are accomplished according to their will.
Although that vidyādhara has attained the most supreme and excellent dharmas,
he constantly brings great benefit to sentient beings,
extensively delivering all classes of living beings and transmitting the flow of the Dharma teachings.
With a mind of equanimity, far removed from love and hatred,
they diligently cultivate practice so that the merit thereby obtained may be universally bestowed upon all sentient beings, causing them all to attain liberation.
In this way, the practitioner shall before long achieve the unsurpassed path of Buddhahood.
Such is the ritual manual spoken by the emanation of Mañjuśrī, the Vidyārāja Yamāntaka.
All Tathāgatas have proclaimed this in unison;
therefore, practitioners and all sentient beings who hear this ritual manual shall no longer harbor any doubt.
By receiving and upholding [this] according to the Dharma, all that is sought shall be accomplished.
